purpose: Leave-one-reference-out back-test measuring how far narration structure alone determines visual treatment.
method: Train additive log-odds priors on three reference documentaries, predict on the held-out fourth. hit@k = the creator's actual treatment set intersects the top k predictions. Baseline = always propose the k most frequent treatments from the training references.
corpus: 628 annotated visual units across 4 reference documentaries

narrationToMediaFamily.note: below baseline; narration structure does not predict which media family to retrieve

ambiguityCeiling.method: For every pair of units sharing an identical feature signature, how often do their treatment sets intersect?

conclusions: Narration structure sharpens the single best guess (0.326 vs 0.188 baseline) but does not determine the treatment.
Two passages with an identical narration contract share a treatment only 44.9% of the time, barely above the 34.2% chance rate.
Knowing the media family raises that agreement to 67.7% and raises top-1 accuracy to 0.406. Available media, not narration structure, is the resolving input.

At four candidates every learned model scored below the always-propose-the-four-most-common baseline. A four-candidate slate must therefore be built for meaningful difference under gate constraints, not by taking the top four scores.
Top-1 reproduction of a creator's choice is the wrong success metric. Slate coverage plus zero gate violations is the defensible one.
